claim: ER O-glycosylation can be induced through relocalisation of GalNAc-Transferases from the Golgi.
source: ER O-glycosylation can be induced through relocalisation GalNAc-Transferases from the Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: ER O-glycosylation markedly stimulates cell migration.
source: This process markedly stimulates cell migration and is constitutively activated in more than 60% of breast carcinomas.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ER O-glycosylation is constitutively activated in more than 60% of breast carcinomas.
source: This process markedly stimulates cell migration and is constitutively activated in more than 60% of breast carcinomas.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by tissue array data in the manuscript.

claim: The screen identified 12 negative regulators of O-glycosylation that all control GalNAc-T sub-cellular localisation.
source: We identified 12 negative regulators of O-glycosylation that all control GalNAc-T sub-cellular localisation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNAi screen presented in the manuscript.

claim: ERK8 is an atypical MAPK with high basal kinase activity.
source: ERK8, an atypical MAPK with high basal kinase activity, is a strong hit and is partially localised at the Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: ERK8 is partially localised at the Golgi.
source: ERK8, an atypical MAPK with high basal kinase activity, is a strong hit and is partially localised at the Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4.

claim: ERK8 inhibition induces the relocation of GalNAc-Ts but not of KDEL receptors.
source: Its inhibition induces the relocation of GalNAc-Ts, but not of KDEL receptors, revealing the existence of two separate COPI-dependent pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in Figure 5E-I.

claim: There exist two separate COPI-dependent pathways for retrograde trafficking.
source: Its inhibition induces the relocation of GalNAc-Ts, but not of KDEL receptors, revealing the existence of two separate COPI-dependent pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of ERK8 on GalNAc-T and KDEL-R trafficking.

claim: ERK8 down-regulation activates cell motility.
source: ERK8 down-regulation, in turn, activates cell motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by wound healing assays in Figure 6.

claim: In human breast and lung carcinomas, ERK8 expression is reduced while ER O-glycosylation initiation is hyperactivated.
source: In human breast and lung carcinomas, ERK8 expression is reduced while ER O-glycosylation initiation is hyperactivated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue microarray analysis in Figure 7.

claim: ERK8 appears as a constitutive brake on GalNAc-T relocalisation.
source: In sum, ERK8 appears as a constitutive brake on GalNAc-T relocalisation, and the loss of its expression could drive cancer aggressivity through increased cell motility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing ERK8 inhibits GalNAc-T relocation.

claim: The loss of ERK8 expression could drive cancer aggressivity through increased cell motility.
source: In sum, ERK8 appears as a constitutive brake on GalNAc-T relocalisation, and the loss of its expression could drive cancer aggressivity through increased cell motility.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed correlation between ERK8 loss and increased Tn in tumors, combined with cell motility data.

claim: O-glycans are synthesised through the step-wise action of various glycosylation enzymes, starting with GalNAc-Ts.
source: O-glycans are synthesised through the step-wise action of various glycosylation enzymes, starting with the UDP-N-Acetyl-Alpha-D-Galactosamine:Polypeptide N-Acetyl-galactosaminyltransferases (GalNAc-Ts), a large family of 20 different isoforms that catalyses the addition of N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto serine or threonine residues (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bennett et al., 2012.

claim: GalNAc-Ts are a large family of 20 different isoforms.
source: O-glycans are synthesised through the step-wise action of various glycosylation enzymes, starting with the UDP-N-Acetyl-Alpha-D-Galactosamine:Polypeptide N-Acetyl-galactosaminyltransferases (GalNAc-Ts), a large family of 20 different isoforms that catalyses the addition of N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto serine or threonine residues (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bennett et al., 2012.

claim: GalNAc-Ts catalyse the addition of N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto serine or threonine residues.
source: O-glycans are synthesised through the step-wise action of various glycosylation enzymes, starting with the UDP-N-Acetyl-Alpha-D-Galactosamine:Polypeptide N-Acetyl-galactosaminyltransferases (GalNAc-Ts), a large family of 20 different isoforms that catalyses the addition of N-Acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto serine or threonine residues (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Bennett et al., 2012.

claim: The addition of GalNAc on proteins generates the Tn antigen.
source: The addition of GalNAc on proteins generates the Tn antigen, with antigenicity being lost upon the addition of other sugar residues.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of glycobiology.

claim: Tn antigenicity is lost upon the addition of other sugar residues.
source: The addition of GalNAc on proteins generates the Tn antigen, with antigenicity being lost upon the addition of other sugar residues.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of glycobiology.

claim: Carcinomas stain prominently with antibodies and lectins such as the Helix Pomatia Lectin (HPL), which binds to Tn antigens.
source: Earlier work demonstrated that carcinomas stain prominently with antibodies and lectins such as the Helix Pomatia Lectin (HPL), which binds to Tn antigens (Springer, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Springer, 1983.

claim: The high prevalence and specificity of the cancer glycophenotype is remarkable, with matching normal tissues and benign tumours expressing much lower levels.
source: The high prevalence and specificity of this cancer glycophenotype is remarkable, with matching normal tissues and benign tumours expressing much lower levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer glycobiology.

claim: The increase in Tn levels is proposed to stem from a block or reduction in the activity of the Core 1 Galactosyl-Transferase (C1GALT).
source: This increase in Tn levels is proposed to stem from a block or reduction in the activity of the main O-GalNAc-modifying enzyme, the Core 1 Galactosyl-Transferase (C1GALT) (Ju et al., 2002a, 2008b; Stanley, 2011); indeed, the loss of C1GALT in the high Tn-expressing T cell leukaemia Jurkat cell line has been reported (Ju et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature cited from multiple sources.

claim: The loss of C1GALT in the high Tn-expressing T cell leukaemia Jurkat cell line has been reported.
source: This increase in Tn levels is proposed to stem from a block or reduction in the activity of the main O-GalNAc-modifying enzyme, the Core 1 Galactosyl-Transferase (C1GALT) (Ju et al., 2002a, 2008b; Stanley, 2011); indeed, the loss of C1GALT in the high Tn-expressing T cell leukaemia Jurkat cell line has been reported (Ju et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is cited from Ju et al., 2008a.

claim: In breast carcinoma, high Tn levels seem to be caused by a different mechanism: GalNAc-Ts are massively relocated from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: In breast carcinoma, however, high Tn levels seem to be caused by a different mechanism: GalNAc-Ts are massively relocated from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) with Tn staining largely located in the ER (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: In breast carcinoma, Tn staining is largely located in the ER.
source: In breast carcinoma, however, high Tn levels seem to be caused by a different mechanism: GalNAc-Ts are massively relocated from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) with Tn staining largely located in the ER (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: In some cancer cells, O-glycosylation initiation in the ER has been reported.
source: Further, in some cancer cells, O-glycosylation initiation in the ER has also been reported (Egea et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from Egea et al., 1993.

claim: Trafficking of GalNAc-Ts to the ER can be stimulated by growth factors such as epidermal growth factor (EGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF).
source: Trafficking of GalNAc-Ts to the ER can be stimulated by growth factors such as epidermal growth factor (EGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), with GalNAc-Ts active in the ER and GalNAc incorporation in proteins increasing after relocation (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2010.

claim: GalNAc-Ts are active in the ER and GalNAc incorporation in proteins increases after relocation.
source: Trafficking of GalNAc-Ts to the ER can be stimulated by growth factors such as epidermal growth factor (EGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), with GalNAc-Ts active in the ER and GalNAc incorporation in proteins increasing after relocation (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2010.

claim: Glycosylation of ER-resident proteins likely explains the observed increase in Tn staining.
source: It is surmised that glycosylation of ER-resident proteins likely explains this observed increase in Tn staining, as several of these proteins bear O-GalNAc in mass spectrometric analyses (Steentoft et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on mass spectrometry data cited from Steentoft et al., 2013.

claim: Several ER-resident proteins bear O-GalNAc in mass spectrometric analyses.
source: It is surmised that glycosylation of ER-resident proteins likely explains this observed increase in Tn staining, as several of these proteins bear O-GalNAc in mass spectrometric analyses (Steentoft et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Steentoft et al., 2013.

claim: O-glycosylation in the ER results in a marked stimulatory effect on cell adhesion and cell migration.
source: Although it is unclear which specific proteins are modified, O-glycosylation in the ER results in a marked stimulatory effect on cell adhesion and cell migration (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: ER O-glycosylation promotes the invasive and metastatic potential of malignant tumour cells.
source: This suggests that ER O-glycosylation promotes the invasive and metastatic potential of malignant tumour cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects on cell migration and adhesion.

claim: Tn levels are consistently higher in higher grade, more aggressive breast tumours.
source: Tn levels are consistently higher in higher grade, more aggressive breast tumours.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer glycobiology.

claim: ER-specific inhibition of O-glycosylation reduced drastically lung metastasis in a mice model.
source: Conversely, ER-specific inhibition of O-glycosylation reduced drastically lung metastasis in a mice model (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: GalNAc-Ts transport is stimulated by activated SRC tyrosine kinases.
source: GalNAc-Ts transport is stimulated by activated SRC tyrosine kinases and requires the COPI coat (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2010.

claim: GalNAc-Ts transport requires the COPI coat.
source: GalNAc-Ts transport is stimulated by activated SRC tyrosine kinases and requires the COPI coat (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2010.

claim: COPI is a multimeric protein complex required for the formation of transport carriers and functions in the retrograde traffic between the Golgi and the ER.
source: COPI is a multimeric protein complex required for the formation of transport carriers and functions in the retrograde traffic between the Golgi and the ER (Beck et al., 2009; Szul and Sztul, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Beck et al., 2009 and Szul and Sztul, 2011.

claim: COPI coat assembly is regulated by small GTPases of the Arf family and their regulator, the GTP exchange factor, GBF1.
source: COPI coat assembly is regulated by small GTPases of the Arf family and their regulator, the GTP exchange factor, GBF1; however, the regulation of COPI-coated carrier formation in response to extracellular signals is poorly understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of membrane trafficking.

claim: The regulation of COPI-coated carrier formation in response to extracellular signals is poorly understood.
source: COPI coat assembly is regulated by small GTPases of the Arf family and their regulator, the GTP exchange factor, GBF1; however, the regulation of COPI-coated carrier formation in response to extracellular signals is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The screen targeted 948 genes presumed to be involved in signal transduction.
source: To better understand the mechanisms regulating Tn expression in cancer, we performed an RNAi screen targeting 948 genes presumed to be involved in signal transduction.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the screen.

claim: ERK8 (alias MAPK15) is the most recently identified member of the MAPK family.
source: We identified and validated 12 regulators, with a particular focus on the MAP kinase ERK8 (alias MAPK15), the most recently identified member of the MAPK family (Abe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Abe et al., 2002.

claim: ERK8 possesses an atypically long C-terminal domain.
source: Unlike classical MAP kinases, ERK8 possesses an atypically long C-terminal domain and appears to constitutively auto-phosphorylate its Thr-X-Tyr motif (Klevernic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Klevernic et al., 2006.

claim: ERK8 appears to constitutively auto-phosphorylate its Thr-X-Tyr motif.
source: Unlike classical MAP kinases, ERK8 possesses an atypically long C-terminal domain and appears to constitutively auto-phosphorylate its Thr-X-Tyr motif (Klevernic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Klevernic et al., 2006.

claim: A fraction of the ERK8 protein is localised at the Golgi where it specifically inhibits COPI vesicle formation and the export of GalNAc-Ts.
source: Here, we find that a fraction of the ERK8 protein is localised at the Golgi where it specifically inhibits COPI vesicle formation and the export of GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The loss of ERK8 activity results in increased O-glycosylation and increased cell motility.
source: The loss of ERK8 activity results in increased O-glycosylation and increased cell motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: ERK8 expression is frequently downregulated in lung carcinomas.
source: We find that ERK8 expression is also frequently downregulated in lung carcinomas, which may partly explain the high Tn phenotype and invasiveness of these tumours.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue microarray analysis in Figure 7.

claim: Knockdown of Syntaxin 5 (STX5) reproducibly induced a 6–7-fold increase in Tn levels relative to a non-targeting control.
source: In a pilot screen using HeLa cells, which targeted 63 known players of membrane traffic (Chia et al., 2012), we identified that knockdown of the SNARE gene Syntaxin 5 (STX5) reproducibly induced a 6–7-fold increase in Tn levels relative to a non-targeting (NT) control (GFP siRNA) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the pilot screen shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The effect of STX5 knockdown on Tn levels was presumably due to a defect in the balance in anterograde vs retrograde ER-to-Golgi traffic of GalNAc-Ts.
source: This effect was presumably due to a defect in the balance in anterograde vs retrograde ER-to-Golgi traffic of GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the STX5 knockdown effect.

claim: 134 siRNA pools reduced the cell number to less than 20% of the control.
source: We discarded the results for 134 siRNA pools that reduced the cell number to less than 20% of the control (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a result from the screen filtering process shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Numerous gene knockdowns increased HPL levels significantly more than STX5 depletion.
source: Of the remaining siRNA pools, we identified numerous gene knockdowns that increased HPL levels significantly more than STX5 depletion.
evidence: This is a result from the screen shown in Figure 1C.

claim: None of the gene depletions significantly reduced the basal levels of Tn in HeLa cells.
source: None of the gene depletions seemed to significantly reduce the basal levels of Tn in HeLa cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the screen shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The knockdown effects were reproduced in independent replicates.
source: The knockdown effects were reproduced in independent replicates (Figure 1–figure supplement 1A), and the trend was mostly independent of the analysis algorithm used, although the fold increase was higher with one method than with the other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The trend in HPL levels was mostly independent of the analysis algorithm used.
source: The knockdown effects were reproduced in independent replicates (Figure 1–figure supplement 1A), and the trend was mostly independent of the analysis algorithm used, although the fold increase was higher with one method than with the other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of ERK8 induced a particularly marked increase in Tn, ranging from 4–25-fold depending on the experimental design and RNAi reagent.
source: Depletion of one of these negative regulators—the Extracellular Signal Regulated Kinase 8 (ERK8)—induced a particularly marked increase in Tn, ranging from 4–25-fold depending on the experimental design and RNAi reagent (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in multiple figures including Figure 1D.

claim: Three out of the four single siRNAs for ERK8 significantly increased Tn levels above the NT control.
source: For ERK8, we observed that three out of the four single siRNAs significantly increased Tn levels above the NT control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Using a threshold of 4.5-fold increase for at least two independent siRNAs, 12 genes were considered validated.
source: Using a threshold of 4.5-fold increase for at least two independent siRNAs, 12 genes were considered validated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is the validation criterion used in the screen.

claim: Knockdown cells stained with Vicia Villosa Lectin (VVL) revealed a highly consistent pattern with HPL staining.
source: To verify that the effects observed were not specific to the detection method used, knockdown cells were also stained with a different lectin, Vicia Villosa Lectin (VVL), which revealed a highly consistent pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: GalNAc-T1 and T2 isoforms are by far the most prevalent and represent most of GalNAc-T activity in HeLa cells.
source: Although GalNAc-Ts represent a large family, the T1 and T2 isoforms are by far the most prevalent and represent most of GalNAc-T activity in HeLa cells (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Bennett et al., 2012.

claim: Depletion of GalNAc-T1 and -T2 resulted in almost complete loss of Tn levels.
source: This is apparent in the almost complete loss of Tn levels when GalNAc-T1 and -T2 were depleted (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Co-depletion of GalNAc-T1 and -T2 significantly reduced the Tn increase from the knockdown of ERK8 as well as that from other Tn regulators.
source: Co-depletion of the two enzymes also reduced significantly the Tn increase from the knockdown of ERK8 as well as that from other Tn regulators (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ERK8 levels were still significantly reduced in the triple knockdown configuration with GalNAc-T1 and -T2.
source: In addition, ERK8 levels were still significantly reduced in the triple knockdown configuration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The loss of expression of C1GALT or its molecular chaperone, COSMC, results in a failure to generate the subsequent Core 1 glycan structure (the TF antigen).
source: The loss of expression of C1GALT or its molecular chaperone, COSMC, results in a failure to generate the subsequent Core 1 glycan structure (the TF antigen) and thus inhibits O-GalNAc extension, which is detectable as a loss in Peanut Agglutinin (PNA) lectin positive staining (Swamy et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Swamy et al., 1991.

claim: Loss of C1GALT or COSMC inhibits O-GalNAc extension, which is detectable as a loss in Peanut Agglutinin (PNA) lectin positive staining.
source: The loss of expression of C1GALT or its molecular chaperone, COSMC, results in a failure to generate the subsequent Core 1 glycan structure (the TF antigen) and thus inhibits O-GalNAc extension, which is detectable as a loss in Peanut Agglutinin (PNA) lectin positive staining (Swamy et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Swamy et al., 1991.

claim: Relocation of GalNAc-Ts from the Golgi apparatus to the ER induces a modest but measurable increase in PNA staining.
source: Relocation of GalNAc-Ts from the Golgi apparatus to the ER, on the other hand, induces a modest but measurable increase in PNA staining (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2010.

claim: HeLa cells with a stable COSMC knockout completely abolished PNA staining.
source: HeLa cells with a stable COSMC knockout which prohibits C1GALT activity, was used as a positive control and, as expected, completely abolished PNA staining.
evidence: This is a control experiment described in the text.

claim: There was either no significant decrease or some increase in PNA staining following depletion of each of the Tn regulators.
source: Comparatively, there was either no significant decrease or some increase in PNA staining following depletion of each of the Tn regulators (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), with the most significant increase in PNA staining observed after ERK8 knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The most significant increase in PNA staining was observed after ERK8 knockdown.
source: Comparatively, there was either no significant decrease or some increase in PNA staining following depletion of each of the Tn regulators (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), with the most significant increase in PNA staining observed after ERK8 knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: None of the Tn-regulating genes appears to be required for core 1-forming activity.
source: Therefore, none of the Tn-regulating genes we identified appears to be required for core 1-forming activity and thus do not regulate Tn levels by inhibiting O-GalNAc extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PNA staining data.

claim: The Tn-regulating genes do not regulate Tn levels by inhibiting O-GalNAc extension.
source: Therefore, none of the Tn-regulating genes we identified appears to be required for core 1-forming activity and thus do not regulate Tn levels by inhibiting O-GalNAc extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PNA staining data.

claim: In control cells, GalNAc-T1 localised exclusively in the perinuclear region, co-localising with the Golgi marker MannII.
source: In control cells, GalNAc-T1 localised exclusively in the perinuclear region, co-localising with the Golgi marker MannII (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon ERK8 depletion, GalNAc-T1 distribution appeared more diffuse, co-localising with the ER marker Calreticulin.
source: Upon ERK8 depletion, GalNAc-T1 distribution appeared more diffuse, co-localising with the ER marker Calreticulin (Figure 2C), with MannII-GFP staining remaining mostly perinuclear (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon ERK8 depletion, MannII-GFP staining remained mostly perinuclear.
source: Upon ERK8 depletion, GalNAc-T1 distribution appeared more diffuse, co-localising with the ER marker Calreticulin (Figure 2C), with MannII-GFP staining remaining mostly perinuclear (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The MannII-GFP-positive structures were more fragmented in ERK8 knockdown cells than in the untreated cells.
source: The MannII-GFP-positive structures were more fragmented in the knockdown cells than in the untreated cells; this finding is reminiscent of the effects of SRC activation (Gill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: Depletion of PI4KA resulted in GalNAc-T1 redistribution.
source: Depletion of phosphatidylinositol (PI) 4-kinase (PI4KA), another major regulator of Tn, also resulted in GalNAc-T1 redistribution (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon PI4KA depletion, MannII-GFP appeared to also redistribute to a cytoplasmic pattern.
source: However, unlike ERK8 depletion, MannII-GFP appeared to also redistribute to a cytoplasmic pattern upon PI4KA depletion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PI4KA depletion suggests that the entire content of the Golgi apparatus becomes redistributed to the ER.
source: This suggests that the entire content of the Golgi apparatus becomes redistributed to the ER, and is consistent with our previous findings, where PI4KA depletion induced a redistribution of TGN46, a trans golgi marker (Chia et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the MannII-GFP redistribution and cited from Chia et al., 2012.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between GalNAc-T1 and Calreticulin was significantly increased following the knockdown of all 12 genes.
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between these two markers was significantly increased following the knockdown of all 12 genes (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most of the 12 Tn regulators exhibited levels of GalNAc-T1/Calreticulin co-localization similar to that induced by Brefeldin A (BFA) treatment.
source: Most exhibited levels similar to that induced by Brefeldin A (BFA) treatment, which redistributes Golgi proteins to the ER (Fujiwara et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a comparison to BFA treatment, cited from Fujiwara et al., 1988.

claim: There was only slight perturbation of GalNAc-T1 localisation in the COSMC knockout cells.
source: Comparatively, there was only slight perturbation of GalNAc-T1 localisation in the COSMC knockout cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: Similar trends in ER relocalisation were observed for GalNAc-T2 staining.
source: Similar trends were also observed for GalNAc-T2 staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: None of the signalling genes significantly affected the MannII-GFP distribution, apart from PI4KA depletion.
source: In contrast to the GalNAc-T staining, none of the signalling genes significantly affected the MannII-GFP distribution, apart from PI4KA depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Signalling genes influence Tn levels through the subcellular distribution of GalNAc-Ts.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that signalling genes influence Tn levels through the subcellular distribution of GalNAc-Ts and that, with the exception of PI4KA, they affect the trafficking of these enzymes specifically.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization data.

claim: With the exception of PI4KA, the signalling genes affect the trafficking of GalNAc-Ts specifically.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that signalling genes influence Tn levels through the subcellular distribution of GalNAc-Ts and that, with the exception of PI4KA, they affect the trafficking of these enzymes specifically.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization data.

claim: PI4KA, PKMYT1 and MAP4K2 have previously been reported to be localised at least partially at the Golgi apparatus.
source: Three proteins—PI4KA, PKMYT1 and MAP4K2—have previously been reported to be localised at least partially at the Golgi apparatus (Nakagawa, 1996; Ren et al., 1996; Liu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: PI4KA is proposed to generate phosphoinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P), which is essential for recruiting membrane trafficking effectors to the Golgi.
source: PI4KA is proposed to generate phosphoinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P), which is essential for recruiting membrane trafficking effectors to the Golgi (De Matteis et al., 2005), including Vps74/GOLPH3, which retains various glycosyltransferases at the Golgi through retrograde trafficking (Wood et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from De Matteis et al., 2005 and Wood et al., 2009.

claim: Vps74/GOLPH3 retains various glycosyltransferases at the Golgi through retrograde trafficking.
source: PI4KA is proposed to generate phosphoinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P), which is essential for recruiting membrane trafficking effectors to the Golgi (De Matteis et al., 2005), including Vps74/GOLPH3, which retains various glycosyltransferases at the Golgi through retrograde trafficking (Wood et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Wood et al., 2009.

claim: PKMYT1 is required for the reassembly of the Golgi during telophase.
source: PKMYT1 is required for the reassembly of the Golgi during telophase (Nakajima et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Nakajima et al., 2008.

claim: ERK8 has been reported to localise perinuclearly in A431 cells.
source: In addition, ERK8 has been reported to localise perinuclearly in A431 cells (Uhlen et al., 2010), suggesting a potential Golgi localisation.
evidence: This is cited from Uhlen et al., 2010.

claim: HIPK3, TTK, MARK2 and DUSP7 interact with Golgi-associated proteins.
source: Four other kinases—HIPK3, TTK, MARK2 and DUSP7— interact with Golgi-associated proteins (Dowd et al., 1998; Colland et al., 2004; Dou et al., 2004; Sowa et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: HIPK3 was found to interact with Golgi structural protein GRASP65, the Golgi-localised LIM kinase, and the ERK8 interactor, HIC-5.
source: HIPK3 was also found to interact with Golgi structural protein GRASP65, the Golgi-localised LIM kinase, and the ERK8 interactor, HIC-5 (Colland et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Colland et al., 2004.

claim: HIPK3 interacts with PKMYT1.
source: HIPK3 also interacts with PKMYT1 (Wells et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Wells et al., 1999.

claim: MARK2 protein controls microtubule stability through phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins.
source: The MARK2 protein controls microtubule stability through phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins (Yoshimura and Miki, 2011) and its interaction with the microtubule tracking protein, CLASP2 (Sowa et al., 2009), suggests CLASP2 as a potential substrate.
evidence: This is cited from Yoshimura and Miki, 2011.

claim: MARK2 interacts with the microtubule tracking protein, CLASP2.
source: The MARK2 protein controls microtubule stability through phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins (Yoshimura and Miki, 2011) and its interaction with the microtubule tracking protein, CLASP2 (Sowa et al., 2009), suggests CLASP2 as a potential substrate.
evidence: This is cited from Sowa et al., 2009.

claim: CLASP2 is involved in microtubule nucleation at the Golgi.
source: CLASP2 is involved in microtubule nucleation at the Golgi (Miller et al., 2009) and microtubules could be nucleated at the cis Golgi (Rivero et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Miller et al., 2009.

claim: Microtubules could be nucleated at the cis Golgi.
source: CLASP2 is involved in microtubule nucleation at the Golgi (Miller et al., 2009) and microtubules could be nucleated at the cis Golgi (Rivero et al., 2009).

claim: GalNAc-T relocation could depend on CLASP2-associated microtubules regulated by MARK2.
source: Since Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic depends on microtubule tracks (Palmer et al., 2005; Spang, 2013), GalNAc-T relocation could depend on CLASP2-associated microtubules regulated by MARK2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known interactions and functions.

claim: ERK8 and TGFBR2 interact with SRC.
source: Two proteins—ERK8 and TGFBR2—interact with SRC (Abe et al., 2002; Galliher and Schiemann, 2007).

claim: ERK8 activity was reported to increase in the presence of active SRC.

claim: TGFBR2 is phosphorylated by SRC.
source: ERK8 activity was reported to increase in the presence of active SRC (Abe et al., 2002) and TGFBR2 is phosphorylated by SRC (Galliher and Schiemann, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Galliher and Schiemann, 2007.

claim: MAP4K2, IKBKE and PPP6C are linked to the canonical NFkB pathway.

claim: The NFkB pathway might control GalNAc-T localisation.
source: In addition, MAP4K2, IKBKE and PPP6C are linked to the canonical NFkB pathway, suggesting that this pathway might control GalNAc-T localisation (Shimada et al., 1999; Chadee et al., 2002; Eddy et al., 2005; Stefansson and Brautigan, 2006).

claim: The Tn-regulating genes are acting at the Golgi level, perhaps part of a regulatory network controlling the subcellular localisation of GalNAc-Ts.

claim: ERK8 displays high basal activity in resting cells and is not stimulated by growth factor activity.
source: ERK8 displays high basal activity in resting cells and is not stimulated by growth factor activity (Abe et al., 2002; Klevernic et al., 2006) but through auto-phosphorylation on residues Thr 175 and Tyr 177.
evidence: This is cited from Abe et al., 2002 and Klevernic et al., 2006.

claim: ERK8 is activated through auto-phosphorylation on residues Thr 175 and Tyr 177.
source: ERK8 displays high basal activity in resting cells and is not stimulated by growth factor activity (Abe et al., 2002; Klevernic et al., 2006) but through auto-phosphorylation on residues Thr 175 and Tyr 177.
evidence: This is cited from Abe et al., 2002 and Klevernic et al., 2006.

claim: Significantly lower HPL staining was observed in cells transfected with the wild-type GFP-ERK8-siR construct compared to non-transfected ERK8-depleted cells.
source: Non-transfected ERK8-depleted cells displayed a marked increase in HPL staining, whereas significantly lower HPL staining was observed in cells transfected with the wild-type GFP-ERK8-siR construct (Figure 3A,B).

claim: HPL levels remained almost similar to non-GFP-expressing ERK8-depleted cells when the cells were transfected with the kinase-inactive mutant (GFP-ERK8-siR-T175A-Y177F).
source: Importantly, HPL levels remained almost similar to non-GFP-expressing ERK8-depleted cells when the cells were transfected with the kinase-inactive mutant (GFP-ERK8-siR-T175A-Y177F) indicating that kinase activity is important for the negative regulation of O-glycosylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Kinase activity is important for the negative regulation of O-glycosylation by ERK8.
source: Importantly, HPL levels remained almost similar to non-GFP-expressing ERK8-depleted cells when the cells were transfected with the kinase-inactive mutant (GFP-ERK8-siR-T175A-Y177F) indicating that kinase activity is important for the negative regulation of O-glycosylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment.

claim: Ro-31-8220 inhibits the kinase activity of ERK8.
source: Ro-31-8220 inhibits the kinase activity of ERK8 (Klevernic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Klevernic et al., 2006.

claim: A significant increase in Tn was observed as early as 1 hr after treatment with 5 µM Ro-31-8220.
source: A significant increase in Tn was observed as early as 1 hr after treatment and peaked at a nearly eightfold increase after 3.5 hr as compared with basal levels (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Tn levels peaked at a nearly eightfold increase after 3.5 hr of Ro-31-8220 treatment.
source: A significant increase in Tn was observed as early as 1 hr after treatment and peaked at a nearly eightfold increase after 3.5 hr as compared with basal levels (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The increase in Tn staining is a relatively rapid phenomenon.
source: This result indicated that the increase in Tn staining is a relatively rapid phenomenon and that O-GalNAc glycosylated protein accumulation can be achieved in a few hours.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rapid kinetics of Tn increase.

claim: O-GalNAc glycosylated protein accumulation can be achieved in a few hours.
source: This result indicated that the increase in Tn staining is a relatively rapid phenomenon and that O-GalNAc glycosylated protein accumulation can be achieved in a few hours.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rapid kinetics of Tn increase.

claim: The changes in Tn were not caused by expression changes of the O-glycoproteins or the O-glycosylation machinery.
source: Our findings also suggest that these changes were not caused by expression changes of the O-glycoproteins or the O-glycosylation machinery.
evidence: This is supported by the transcription inhibitor experiment and protein level analysis.

claim: Co-treatment of cells with Ro-31-8220 and a transcriptional inhibitor α-amanitin did not reduce Tn levels.
source: Indeed, co-treatment of cells with Ro-31-8220 and a transcriptional inhibitor α-amanitin (Chafin et al., 1995) did not reduce Tn levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and protein levels of the enzymes and chaperones involved in the early O-glycosylation stages were unaffected in ERK8-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Protein levels of the enzymes and chaperones involved in the early O-glycosylation stages were unaffected in ERK8-depleted cells.
source: Indeed, co-treatment of cells with Ro-31-8220 and a transcriptional inhibitor α-amanitin (Chafin et al., 1995) did not reduce Tn levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and protein levels of the enzymes and chaperones involved in the early O-glycosylation stages were unaffected in ERK8-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The rapid effect of Ro-31-8220 suggests that ERK8 acts relatively directly on GalNAc-T traffic.
source: The rapid effect of Ro-31-8220 suggests that ERK8 acts relatively directly on GalNAc-T traffic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rapid kinetics of the inhibitor effect.

claim: There was a significant increase in the glycosylation of the ER-specific glycosylation reporter (GFP-Muc-PTS) upon treatment with Ro-31-8220 for 3.5 hr.
source: After pulldown with HPL-conjugated beads, we found a significant increase in the glycosylation of this reporter upon treatment with Ro-31-8220 for 3.5 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: An ER-localised GalNAc-T inhibitor counteracted the increase in Tn levels observed upon ERK8 knockdown.
source: We also verified ER localisation using a stably expressed ER-localised GalNAc-T inhibitor described previously (Gill et al., 2013). This inhibitor counteracted the increase in Tn levels observed upon ERK8 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells depleted of ERK8 (by siRNA or Ro-31-8220) exhibited substantial increases in GalNAz incorporation.
source: After 24 hr, cells depleted of ERK8 (by siRNA or Ro-31-8220) exhibited substantial increases in GalNAz incorporation, as revealed by the presence of several bands on SDS-PAGE gels (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ERK8 controls the O-glycosylation status of several proteins, which probably includes ER residents.
source: This suggests that ERK8 controls the O-glycosylation status of several proteins, which probably includes ER residents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolic labeling data.

claim: High Tn levels obtained after 3.5 hr of Ro-31-8220 treatment decreased progressively with an approximately 2.5-hr half-life after drug washout.
source: High Tn levels obtained after 3.5 hr of treatment decreased progressively with an approximately 2.5-hr half-life (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: GalNAc-T staining showed a significant increase in enzyme localisation at the Golgi within 2 hr of Ro-31-8220 washout.
source: Consistently, staining for GalNAc-Ts showed a similar trend, with a significant increase in enzyme localisation at the Golgi within 2 hr of washout (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Reactivation of ERK8 slows the continuous retrograde flow of GalNAc-Ts and anterograde traffic shifts their distribution back to the Golgi.
source: This suggests that reactivation of ERK8 slows the continuous retrograde flow of GalNAc-Ts and that anterograde traffic shifts their distribution back to the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the washout experiment.

claim: GalNAc-T relocalisation is rapidly reversible.
source: These results show that GalNAc-T relocalisation is rapidly reversible and suggests that ERK8 provides a continual brake for GalNAc-T relocation at the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the washout experiment.

claim: ERK8 provides a continual brake for GalNAc-T relocation at the Golgi.
source: These results show that GalNAc-T relocalisation is rapidly reversible and suggests that ERK8 provides a continual brake for GalNAc-T relocation at the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the washout experiment.

claim: GalNAc-Ts are thought to regularly cycle between the ER and the Golgi apparatus.
source: GalNAc-Ts are thought to regularly cycle between the ER and the Golgi apparatus (Rhee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Rhee et al., 2005.

claim: Prolonged permeabilisation (2 hr) clearly revealed positive Golgi staining for ERK8.
source: However, prolonged permeabilisation (2 hr) clearly revealed positive Golgi staining, suggesting that a fraction of ERK8 is associated with this organelle (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A fraction of ERK8 is associated with the Golgi organelle.
source: However, prolonged permeabilisation (2 hr) clearly revealed positive Golgi staining, suggesting that a fraction of ERK8 is associated with this organelle (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HeLa cells stimulated with 50 ng/µl of PDGF showed an increase in HPL staining intensity between 30 min and 2 hr.
source: Next, HeLa cells were stimulated with 50 ng/µl of PDGF, resulting in an increase in HPL staining intensity between 30 min and 2 hr and a decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi apparatus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HeLa cells stimulated with PDGF showed a decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi apparatus.
source: Next, HeLa cells were stimulated with 50 ng/µl of PDGF, resulting in an increase in HPL staining intensity between 30 min and 2 hr and a decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi apparatus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a 60% decrease in the Pearson's Correlation coefficient of ERK8 and TGN46 staining after 2 hr of PDGF treatment.
source: Using the Pearson's Correlation coefficient of ERK8 and TGN46 staining, we found a 60% decrease after 2 hr, suggesting that ERK8 is displaced from the Golgi after cell stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ERK8 is displaced from the Golgi after cell stimulation with PDGF.
source: Using the Pearson's Correlation coefficient of ERK8 and TGN46 staining, we found a 60% decrease after 2 hr, suggesting that ERK8 is displaced from the Golgi after cell stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation coefficient data.

claim: SRC is a key signal transducer between PDGF and GalNAc-T traffic.
source: SRC is a key signal transducer between PDGF and GalNAc-T traffic.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A gradual decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi was observed in cells expressing Src-8A7F-mCherry treated with imidazole.
source: Using a HeLa cell line stably expressing Src-8A7F-mCherry, we observed a gradual decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas no change was observed with a catalytically defective SRC mutant (Src 6N7F) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: No change in ERK8 at the Golgi was observed with a catalytically defective SRC mutant (Src 6N7F).
source: Using a HeLa cell line stably expressing Src-8A7F-mCherry, we observed a gradual decrease in ERK8 at the Golgi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas no change was observed with a catalytically defective SRC mutant (Src 6N7F) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SRC activity regulates ERK8 localisation at the Golgi.
source: This suggests that SRC activity regulates ERK8 localisation at the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRC mutant experiments.

claim: ERK8 is dynamically localised at the Golgi apparatus where it likely controls GalNAc-T export.
source: Overall, our data indicate that ERK8 is dynamically localised at the Golgi apparatus where it likely controls GalNAc-T export.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization and functional data.

claim: Expression of the dominant-negative mutant of Arf1(Q71L) provided significant rescue of Tn levels in ERK8-depleted cells.
source: To test if the relocation of GalNAc-Ts in ERK8-depleted cells is dependent on COPI, we first expressed the dominant-negative mutant of Arf1(Q71L), which is unable to hydrolyse bound GTP (Dascher and Balch, 1994) and found significant rescue of Tn levels in contrast with cells expressing wild-type Arf1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with 50 nM of the GBF1 inhibitor Golgicide provided significant rescue of Tn levels in ERK8-depleted cells.
source: ERK8-depleted cells were also treated with 50 nM of the GBF1 inhibitor Golgicide (Saenz et al., 2009), which also provided significant rescue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Combined knockdown of ERK8 and GBF1 almost completely reversed high HPL staining.
source: Consistent with these results, combined knockdown of ERK8 and GBF1 almost completely reversed high HPL staining, further indicating that GBF1 is required for GalNAc-T relocation from the Golgi to the ER (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GBF1 is required for GalNAc-T relocation from the Golgi to the ER.
source: Consistent with these results, combined knockdown of ERK8 and GBF1 almost completely reversed high HPL staining, further indicating that GBF1 is required for GalNAc-T relocation from the Golgi to the ER (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-knockdown experiment.

claim: Co-knockdown of ERK8 with Arf1, -3, -4 or -5 reduced Tn levels by about 60%.
source: Co-knockdown of ERK8 with Arf1, -3, -4 or -5 also reduced Tn levels by about 60% (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Combined knockdowns of Arfs further increased the rescue of Tn levels, suggesting functional redundancy amongst the Arf proteins.
source: Combined knockdowns of Arfs further increased the rescue, suggesting functional redundancy amongst the Arf proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-knockdown data.

claim: Co-knockdown of ERK8 with Arf6 did not affect Tn levels.
source: By contrast, co-knockdown with Arf6, which does not regulate COPI, did not affect Tn levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The COPI trafficking machinery is essential for the ER relocation of GalNAc-Ts.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the COPI trafficking machinery is essential for the ER relocation of GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Arf and GBF1 co-knockdown experiments.

claim: Arf1-GTP loading was activated as early as 15 min after ERK8 inhibition using Ro-31-8220 and sustained for over 2 hr.
source: Therefore, we assessed Arf1-GTP loading after ERK8 inhibition using Ro-31-8220 and found activation of Arf1 as early as 15 min and sustained for over 2 hr (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: COPB staining was significantly more affected than GM130 staining after ERK8 depletion and found on small structures in the cytoplasm, suggesting enrichment on transport intermediates.
source: Interestingly, COPB staining was significantly more affected and found on small structures in the cytoplasm, suggesting enrichment on transport intermediates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was a nearly 4-fold increase in distribution for COPB but only slightly more than a twofold increase for GM130 after ERK8 depletion.
source: Using a granularity measurement algorithm, we found a nearly 4-fold increase in distribution for COPB but only slightly more than a twofold increase for GM130 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cells treated with Ro-31-8220 displayed a significant redistribution of COPI coatomer staining as early as 5 min after treatment.
source: When treated with the ERK8 inhibitor Ro-31-8220, cells displayed a significant redistribution of COPI coatomer staining as early as 5 min after treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: In cells inhibited by Ro-31-8220 for 15 min, numerous COPI-positive vesicular structures were clearly co-stained with GalNAc-T1 antibodies.
source: Furthermore, in cells inhibited by Ro-31-8220 for 15 min, numerous COPI-positive vesicular structures were clearly co-stained with GalNAc-T1 antibodies (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Tubular structures emanating from the Golgi apparatus stained positively for GalNAc-T1 as well as COPB.
source: In several instances, we could detect tubular structures emanating from the Golgi apparatus that stained positively for GalNAc-T1 as well as COPB, although not as homogenously along their length as for seen for GalNAc-T1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ERK8 depletion did not detectably affect KDEL-R distribution in cells where GalNAc-T relocation was extensive.
source: However, we found that ERK8 depletion did not detectably affect KDEL-R distribution in cells where GalNAc-T relocation was extensive (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Expression of an active form of SRC (E378G; SrcE) similarly relocated GalNAc-T1 to the ER and also strongly affected KDEL-R-GFP distribution.
source: By contrast, expression of an active form of SRC (E378G; SrcE) similarly relocated GalNAc-T1 to the ER, as compared with inactive SRC (K295M; SrcK) but it also strongly affected KDEL-R-GFP distribution (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: More than 80% of cells expressing SrcE display relocation for both GalNAc-T1 and KDEL-R.
source: Visual scoring of the localisation of KDEL-R and GalNAc-T1 revealed than more than 80% of the cells display relocation for both proteins in SrcE expressing cells.
evidence: This is a result from visual scoring shown in Figure 5G.

claim: More than 70% of ERK8 depleted cells exhibit clear GalNAc-T redistribution from the Golgi, while less than 20% show KDEL-R relocation.
source: By contrast, while more than 70% of ERK8 depleted cells exhibit clear GalNAc-T redistribution from the Golgi, less than 20% show KDEL-R relocation (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G.

claim: GalNAc-Ts and KDEL-R trafficking are differentially regulated.
source: These results indicate that GalNAc-Ts and KDEL-R trafficking are differentially regulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of ERK8 and SRC on the two proteins.

claim: When a wave of VSVG was induced by temperature shift, KDEL-R was relocated from the Golgi to the ER whereas GalNAc-Ts were not affected.
source: Consistent with this observation, when a wave of the temperature-sensitive mutant of the vesicular stomatitis virus G glycoprotein (VSVG) was induced by temperature shift, KDEL-R was relocated from the Golgi to the ER as previously reported (Figure 5H; Pulvirenti et al., 2008), whereas GalNAc-Ts were not affected (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: SRC stimulates both GalNAc-Ts and KDEL-R COPI-dependent retrograde traffic.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that SRC stimulates both GalNAc-Ts and KDEL-R COPI-dependent retrograde traffic whereas ERK8 inhibits specifically the formation of transport intermediates containing GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of SRC and ERK8.

claim: ERK8 inhibits specifically the formation of transport intermediates containing GalNAc-Ts.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that SRC stimulates both GalNAc-Ts and KDEL-R COPI-dependent retrograde traffic whereas ERK8 inhibits specifically the formation of transport intermediates containing GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of SRC and ERK8.

claim: O-glycosylation in the ER stimulates cell adhesion and cell migration and tends to induce a spindle-shaped morphology.
source: O-glycosylation in the ER stimulates cell adhesion and cell migration and tends to induce a spindle-shaped morphology (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: A spindle-shaped morphology was apparent in ERK8-depleted HeLa cells under phase contrast microscopy and after staining for the actin and tubulin cytoskeletons.
source: Interestingly, this morphology was also apparent in ERK8-depleted HeLa cells under phase contrast microscopy (Figure 6A) and after staining for the actin and tubulin cytoskeletons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: ERK8-depleted HeLa cells migrated about twofold faster into the denuded area compared with NT siRNA-treated cells in a scratch-wound healing assay.
source: When tested on fibronectin-coated plates in a scratch-wound healing assay, ERK8-depleted HeLa cells migrated about twofold faster into the denuded area compared with NT siRNA-treated cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The faster wound closure rate in ERK8-depleted cells was constant over 7 hr.
source: This faster rate was constant over 7 hr (Figure 6D), indicating that the faster wound closure is caused by faster cell migration and not enhanced reactivity to the initial wound.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The faster wound closure in ERK8-depleted cells is caused by faster cell migration and not enhanced reactivity to the initial wound.
source: This faster rate was constant over 7 hr (Figure 6D), indicating that the faster wound closure is caused by faster cell migration and not enhanced reactivity to the initial wound.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the constant rate of wound closure.

claim: ERK8 knockdown led to a dramatically higher cell surface Tn staining, with numerous Tn-positive protrusion structures.
source: ERK8 knockdown also led to a dramatically higher cell surface Tn staining, with numerous Tn-positive protrusion structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tn-bearing glycoproteins are likely to promote increased cell adhesion.
source: These Tn-bearing glycoproteins are likely to promote increased cell adhesion, as shown previously (Gill et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gill et al., 2013.

claim: Cells co-knocked down for ERK8 and GalNAc-T1 and -T2 migrated significantly slower than ERK8 and ERK8+NT knockdown cells and were similar to NT control cells.
source: We found that these cells migrated significantly slower than ERK8 and ERK8+NT knockdown cells and were similar to NT control cells (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell migration rates induced by ERK8 depletion in Lec2GFP cells were significantly reduced compared with cells expressing only GFP (NGFP cells).
source: Cell migration rates induced by ERK8 depletion in Lec2GFP cells were significantly reduced compared with cells expressing only GFP (NGFP cells) (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and, again, were rather similar to NT control cell migration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Lec2GFP construct itself did not significantly slow cell migration in the absence of ERK8 depletion.
source: It is important to note that the Lec2GFP construct itself did not significantly slow cell migration in the absence of ERK8 depletion.
evidence: This is a control observation from the migration assay.

claim: ERK8 is a negative regulator of cell migration through inhibition of protein O-glycosylation in the ER.
source: Thus, collectively, our results indicate that ERK8 is a negative regulator of cell migration through inhibition of protein O-glycosylation in the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the migration assays with GalNAc-T and Lec2GFP co-knockdowns.

claim: ERK8 protein levels are reported to be fairly constant in normal breast tissue and benign tumours but drop significantly in malignant tumours.
source: Interestingly, ERK8 protein levels are reported to be fairly constant in normal breast tissue and benign tumours but drop significantly in malignant tumours, with a loss measured in approximately 50%, 80% and 100% of grade 1, 2 and 3 tumours, respectively (Henrich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Henrich et al., 2003.

claim: ERK8 loss is measured in approximately 50%, 80% and 100% of grade 1, 2 and 3 breast tumours, respectively.
source: Interestingly, ERK8 protein levels are reported to be fairly constant in normal breast tissue and benign tumours but drop significantly in malignant tumours, with a loss measured in approximately 50%, 80% and 100% of grade 1, 2 and 3 tumours, respectively (Henrich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Henrich et al., 2003.

claim: Henrich et al. proposed that ERK8 stimulates the degradation of Oestrogen Receptor-alpha.
source: Henrich et al. proposed that ERK8 stimulates the degradation of Oestrogen Receptor-alpha, suggesting a possible selective advantage for the loss of this MAPK (Henrich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Henrich et al., 2003.

source: Interestingly, this trend is also consistent with the increased frequency and intensity of Tn staining (Gill et al., 2013).

evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

source: In most cores, ERK8 and Tn levels appeared to show opposing trends, suggesting that the loss of ERK8 could partially drive high Tn expression.

claim: The loss of ERK8 could partially drive high Tn expression in breast tumors.
source: In most cores, ERK8 and Tn levels appeared to show opposing trends, suggesting that the loss of ERK8 could partially drive high Tn expression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the opposing trends observed.

claim: There was no clear correlation between the levels of ERK8 and Tn in breast tumor cores.
source: However, there was no clear correlation between the levels of both antigens (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was an average 80% loss of ERK8 expression in lung carcinomas, with a range of 40–90%.
source: We found that ERK8 was clearly detectable in normal tissues but that the levels appeared markedly lower in all lung carcinomas (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H), with an average 80% loss of expression, and a range of 40–90% (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 18 lung carcinoma cores (86%) displayed higher than normal levels of Tn.
source: Next, we quantified Tn levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F) and found a significantly higher expression of Tn in a majority of the samples, with a more than fourfold average higher expression (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I) and a range of 2–10-fold; 18 cores (86%) displayed higher than normal levels of Tn (Figure 7D).
